clinicalPearls: The commonest inherited neutrophil enzyme defect, yet most affected individuals are clinically asymptomatic because alternative oxygen-dependent and oxygen-independent killing mechanisms compensate
Caused by variants in the MPO gene and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, producing either complete or partial enzyme deficiency
Myeloperoxidase generates hypochlorous acid and other reactive halogen species from hydrogen peroxide and chloride within the phagolysosome, a potent microbicidal system
The defect is frequently discovered incidentally when peroxidase-based automated haematology analysers flag absent neutrophil and eosinophil peroxidase activity
Clinically significant infection is uncommon, but there is a recognised predisposition to invasive candidiasis, including Candida sepsis, particularly when diabetes mellitus coexists
The NADPH oxidase respiratory burst is intact, which distinguishes myeloperoxidase deficiency from chronic granulomatous disease on nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine testing
Most individuals need no specific treatment, so management focuses on prompt recognition and treatment of fungal infection in those at risk
reference.pathophysiology: Myeloperoxidase is a haem-containing enzyme stored in the azurophilic (primary) granules of neutrophils and in monocyte lysosomes. After phagocytosis it is discharged into the phagosome, where it uses hydrogen peroxide generated by the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst together with chloride to form hypochlorous acid and related reactive species that kill ingested microbes. Inherited deficiency removes this halogenation system, but killing mediated by hydrogen peroxide itself, defensins and other granule constituents remains largely intact, which explains the generally mild phenotype. Killing of fungi, particularly Candida hyphae, is more dependent on the myeloperoxidase system, accounting for the specific vulnerability to invasive candidiasis, an effect amplified by hyperglycaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Severe glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with granulocyte dysfunction
Other causes of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
Acquired myeloperoxidase deficiency due to myelodysplasia, drugs or heavy-metal exposure
additionalInvestigations: Peroxidase cytochemical stain on the blood film showing absent neutrophil activity
Automated analyser peroxidase channel demonstrating absent granulocyte peroxidase
Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium test, normal results excluding chronic granulomatous disease
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin to detect coexisting diabetes
Fungal cultures and imaging when invasive candidiasis is suspected
Neutrophil bactericidal and functional assays if the phenotype is atypical
redFlags: Invasive or disseminated candidiasis, especially in a person with diabetes
Deep fungal infection or Candida bloodstream infection
Severe or recurrent infection suggesting an additional or alternative immune defect
Unexplained absence of neutrophil peroxidase in the context of active infection
reference.prognosis: The great majority of individuals have a normal life expectancy with no excess infection burden, so the overall prognosis is excellent; clinically important risk is largely confined to invasive fungal infection in those with concurrent diabetes or additional immune compromise.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting an incidental analyser flag as myelodysplasia or a laboratory artefact
Confusing myeloperoxidase deficiency with chronic granulomatous disease despite the normal respiratory burst
Assuming that every inherited neutrophil defect is clinically significant
Overlooking coexisting diabetes that heightens candidal risk
Failing to consider acquired myeloperoxidase deficiency in the setting of myelodysplasia
